reviews.text: Once Upon a Galaxy is a dazzling gem in the world of autobattlers. A game that effortlessly blends fast-paced strategy, rich fantasy lore, and vibrant cosmic flair. Whether you're a seasoned tactician or a casual gamer, this free-to-play card battler offers an addictive loop of deck-building, discovery, and domination among the stars. Gameplay is smooth and snappy. Matches are quick yet layered with strategic depth, positioning, timing, and synergy matter greatly, but never bog down the pace. The autobattler format is accessible, but there’s room for real mastery. As your crew grows, you'll discover unique combos and unexpected counters that keep every match feeling fresh and dynamic.

Fun free to play game. Pick a captain, every round pick a character, watch your plans fall apart, and still end up in the top 3. Good progression, fun grind, easy gameplay.

It's a good adaptation of the mobile game. It also has NO ads, and all the mtx are optional - It's not in-your-face at all. If you're looking for an auto-battler that has a unique feel and "broken-feeling" (but actually counter-able) mechanics, this is it.

TLDR: Gameplay, strategy, variety, art, design, etc are 9.5+ out of 10 and it can be very very fun. But...the matchmaking & ranking systems are a 0.1 out of 10 and really kills any potential it has to be great. I have most of my time played on mobile but wanted to try the pc version, and it's been the same experience so far. The Good: Especially early on the game is so much fun to play. The deck building/store system is great and well-designed with a lot of deck variety and treasure options to keep every run feeling fresh and new. The gameplay is fast-paced and with very little "wasted" time (especially after the Hunt bug fix). The themes and art for the cards are on point and really add to the enjoyment, and it isn't pay to win. The Bad: The matchmaking system is so incredibly bad, it feels very much like a rubber band style system(which is already bad) but executed in the worst ways possible. For example, early on it's nearly impossible to finish anywhere but 1st place unless you're really trying hard to lose. Your first 50+ runs will be a win every single time. This is made even worse by the ranking system where early on it takes something like 3 or 4 losses to negate a win so there's really no feeling of accomplishment when you rank up. Hitting legendary takes 0 skill, you just have to play enough games and it's guaranteed. Once you're legendary you get to feel the other end of the rubber band, where the majority of your runs are 100% unwinnable regardless of your card selections or strategy. You might be having one of the luckiest drafts you've ever had with a full board of 50/50s on turn 3, but you'll just end up facing the deck in your pod that *somehow* has 10,000/10,000s on turn 4. Having every hero and every card is nice but still ultimately doesn't matter because you often won't even see the cards from your deck in the draft, and even if you do it still won't save you when the matchmaking decides that your pod is unwinnable. So it's really not worth dropping the few thousand dollars, just earn them slow and steady for free. Another massive downside is that the **Leaderboard** is only based on wins. So because of the atrocious matchmaking system.. it's just full of people that win a run normally and then intentionally lose a handful of times to lower their rating(permanently staying in the unloseable zone), rinse and repeat ad nauseam. You have an MMR rating that you can use to gauge how well you're actually doing, and eventually a rank once you inevitably hit legendary.. but those don't really matter at all as there's no legitimate leaderboard for it. And if you ever do get top 10 or 20 legendary, you need to win about 5 or 6 runs to negate a single loss, which again is almost entirely out of your control anyway so it comes down 100% to luck. (Some luck is good in games obviously, but a matchmaking system based entirely on it is awful). I would have left a neutral review if there was an option, the game itself is actually really great, and I would happily recommend it to someone who wants something free to enjoy for a few hours. The matchmaking/ranking just really holds it back. I hope they continue to work on or even completely overhaul both systems, and maybe focus less on getting new hero artwork$ out there. /rant

Good game but stay away until they fix the game breaking bugs. Example: I just played a game and on turn I faced off against the time skipper captain and he had a full board of characters... on turn freaking two... The captain that skips the first turn had a full board of characters on turn two! That's not even possible with a normal captain let alone the captain that skips the first turn. BROKEN.

Fun game, but the AI controlled opponents as you rank up will almost always have better stuff than you; frequently in ways that shouldn't be possible (like having a full board on turn 2, King Midas having full hearts on turn 1, Indiana Clones having a secret rare on turn 5, etc). I get that a simple game AI isn't ever going to be as strong as a player--and that they therefore have to be given an advantage--but it can get frustrating real quick. Also, half of the captains are completely useless, half of the remainder are just OK, and the last quarter are grossly overpowered. There are some SERIOUS balancing issues that need to be looked at. If you built a tier list, you'd only need S, C, and F tiers. If the balancing can be addressed, and if the AI can be tuned away from "HULK SMASH" then this game could easily be spectacular. For now, it's just a cutesy Runeterra wannabe. That said, I *do* enjoy it, and so do my kids who play with me.

OK, 45+ Hours played, and I have some warnings for you friends, This is another game in a growing list of recent games that follow certain VERY disturbing patterns. There have been quite a few of these lately, as somebody who has 1K+ hours in the Bazaar, I know all too well. These games are insanely addictive, to the point where you will ask yourself why, and you won't have any answer, except for that it is "fun" to play. Thing is, as you play more, you will experience the same thing in these games. At first you will think "I just need to get better" because you start losing so much. Keep playing, and it will seem like you gradually improve. What a fantastic feeling! I'm playing a fun game and slowly getting better? What could go wrong here? Well, in all these games, without exception, you will reach the point where you are at a rank/MMR/whatever term the game uses, where winning seems like an impossibility. Where it just becomes a soul-crushing experience of building an amazing build, only to time and time again get matched against builds that are literally unbeatable. Insane builds, comletely broken stuff. This will have you start questioning yourself, will have you rage at the game, wil have you rage at yourself and will leave you in a state of constant hesitation and anxiety. This is what the game is designed to do. Because at this point, without you realizing, you now actually CARE about this game, the results and your winrate. They have you in a spot where they can artificially rope you forever, controlling winrate, matchmaking and basically potentially rigging any and every part of your experience without you ever knowing, because Dark Patterns used by the gambling industry are not yet banned by Steam or any governments. MAKE NO MISTAKE, This game is one of a new generation, using sugarcoated candylike art (just like CandyCrush back in the day) and the air of whimsyness and various behavioral/psychological manipulation technqiues to get you addicted to a game that has no right to even be taken seriously. These games are designed to manipulate you from the start, by giving you a completely fabricated experience, controlling wins, losses, draws and matchmaking in every single way at every single point of the way, carefully crafting a very calculated "experience" for the user. Making them go through lows and highs, slowly reprogramming the end users expectations, exeriences and making any "progress" completely arbitrary and fake. This is not a conspiracy theory or anything, just see for yourself if you don't believe me. You'll experience it all for yourself. You won't enjoy it. I'm not the only one who is of this opinion, check other reviews concerning balance/matchmaking. People with hundreds of hours share this experience. These good folks are under the impression that balance is off, or that matchmaking is "broken". They fail to realise it is all intentional. They already adapted new/different monetization, scrubbing their site of previous entires about cosmetic only mtx and such. It's just a whole bag of red flags. STAY AWAY. And be aware of these new games that abuse manipulative tactics like this.

I played for 22 hours. It's a Super Auto Pets clone with nothing original whatsoever, but ok fine. Then the developer posts an update that literally erases all of my progress as well as others. It wasn't a bug or a mistake -- they did it on purpose because they changed their mind about what should be achieveable and what should be free. I wrote a post about it. No curse words, no insults, no rude tone, nothing. Just basically "You erased all my progress! :( and could you please fix it or allow me to reset my account." And their response ... was to BAN ME FROM THEIR FORUMS. Lol ???? I have been designing games and logical systems for 25 years. I have published several games and managed my own projects' customer support at various points as well. I have been on Steam over a decade, where I've played hundreds of games in this genre and have always been an active member of the community. The number of times I've even been WARNED about comments is zero. Developers that behave this way towards their players -- erasing all their progress haphazardly and then literally BANNING THEM rather than dealing with the problem or even acknowledging what they've done ... well, I don't know what to say. I guess you can decide for yourself whether you want to play a game in this environment. Good luck to you if you do. (By the way, you should really just play Super Auto Pets if you like this kind of game -- why support the complete rip-off that has nothing new?) I genuinely posted this review to try to warn people and I hope it is helpful to you. Cheers, Sir V

A bit of harmless fun, but nowhere near the depth of other autobattlers, even though it tries to trick the player. Good for the extreme casual player, who doesn't want to think much, yet still wants some feeling of "progress" and "skill expression", even though it's entirely fabricated and mostly fake. Game suggests there are multiplayer lobbies, but instead it uses "snapshots" of other people's boards, and then applies further number tweaking depending on the rank you're at and your last runs. It a form of "forced 50%" to make sure every player will win a good amount of the time. There are no interactions between actual players, your board doesn't influence theirs. Instead the game boosts the appearance of synergies you are building, regardless of what you choose. But not the same every game, if you're "due" a win you will be swimming in good options, but if you just won, you might not see anything useful in the shops. All those behind the scenes numbers are unknown and developers will not share them (or admit anything other than this being an actual multiplayer skill based autobattler). This is just a pure time waster, no skill required, just time. The game will make sure you get your wins. My estimation is that the player input is responsible for less than 50% for sure, and probably less than 25%, of the outcomes of the game (unless you intentionally try to lose). Majority of the time, even with the best planning, theorycrafting and plays, the outcome has already been decided by what "snapshots" you were matched with, based entirely on their algorithm that tries to make everyone win a certain % of the time.

Starts out strong, but random chance and unbalanced matchmaking quickly kills any chance of decent runs. Many characters are op, and can almost immediately steamroll. You'll have fun for the first 100 games, but quickly realize the games are rigged as you'll go second ten rounds in a row while attacking the only character you won't be able to beat. I used to think the attacks were random, but it very obviously notices when you are winning, and aims to make you lose to keep playing until you win. You'll spend most of the time playing this game getting annihilated in the first 5 rounds while going up against fully stacked teams. If it ever got balanced, and quit with the artificial difficulty mobile game garbage this would be a much better game. All this becomes more and more apparent as you play longer, and it just isn't fun anymore.

I struggled for a little while to decide how to rate the game. As usual, it's unfortunate that we only get this binary choice. I think I might have rated it more like 3/5. I like a lot about the game and I have certainly played it a lot. However, it has some critical flaws which frequently anger me and which may make me stop if not addressed. These aren't small things. They're pretty fundamental to how the game works. The core issue is just how easy it is to die quickly and feel like there wasn't much you could do about it. So what causes this? 1. The health system: You get 3 hearts. A loss by 2 units or less deals half a heart of damage. However, a loss of 3 or more deals a full heart. 3 hearts is NOT a lot, especially at higher ranks. If you get unlucky you can die as early as turn 4. You could finally get to an inflection point where you might be able to stabilize only to run into a single high roller and die on the spot. The lack of time you have to see shops and make decisions about your build can make the game feel really random at times. And the decision to make you lose more if you lose by a lot just punishes you even harder for running into a highroller. This is the problem that creates the pressure which makes all other problems worse. 2. The way the asynchronous multiplayer works is... suspicious. You aren't fighting real players as they play the game with you like you would in HS BG. You can take as much time as you like to take your turn, (which I like for the record) meaning the game has some way of saving or generating boards based on other players for you to go against at various turns of the game. We have no way to prove this, but many players and I have talked about encountering boards which are wildly too strong for the turn they appear on. Some of these may just be absurd highrolls, but some seem practically impossible. Not only does this create unfair matchups, combined with the health system, it has the potential to knock you out of the game before you have any chance to catch up, if that's even possible. 3. The way silvers/golds/bonus shops work creates a lot of variance. When you see another copy of a card you've already bought, it's silver. This gives you a slight upgrade, moves you one step towards the golden upgrade, and most importantly, it gives you a bonus shop. For the most part, you have little to no control over when this happens, especially in the early game, which is also when even those small stat boosts from silvering can make a huge difference in fight outcomes. So if someone gets lucky and hits a few silvers in the first few turns, or god forbid, a golden, they can end up so far ahead of you that not only are you always going to lose to them, you may even take a full heart in damage. The earliest you can lose a full heart is turn 2 when the opponent can have 4 units on the board. Starting the game off down 1/3rd of your life before you have any meaningful chance to make decisions is absurd. And of course, often these advantages compound. An early golden support might let you get some hunt triggers you otherwise couldn't have, etc. 4. Some heroes are just straight up too weak. Even if they could be good in theory given enough time and the right strategy, in practice you rarely have that time before you just die to someone playing something that gives them straightforward, immediate value. Which is a shame, because a lot of those weaker heroes have some fun designs. Lastly, unrelated to the above issues, I just wanted to address the business model and how it affects the game. Things like roguelikes, autobattlers, etc. are meant to be something where you can enter a run with no initial preparation and expect to have a novel experience due to the random outcomes within the run. This game has made the choice to have each hero have an 8 card deck which they bring in to the match with them that is added to the overall card pool so that you can bend your strategy in one particular direction. In order to get these cards, you must unlock them by either grinding A LOT (I have played for many many hours now and yet I don't have a full set of cards for ANY of the heroes.) or by spending money on theme decks or a premium battle pass. And for reference they are definitely going for the absurd pricing that many F2P CCGs go for. For reference, there is an option to spend $100 on a gem purchase. I'm sorry, any F2P indie game where you can spend more than a full priced AAA and still not have everything is absurd. We should never have tolerated this in this industry. Anyway, beyond the business model, the actual deck mechanic creates some friction to being able to just queue up and start a match and reduces they potential for varied games. They've obviously made this design for the business model and in the process they have made a worse designed game than they could have. For the most part, I have avoided engaging with the deck building mechanics, but especially as I reach higher ranks, I have become more aware of the degree to which I am at a disadvantage by not creating my own deck. In general I just don't want to have to do that and that feeling is increased by the fact that I'm missing a lot of the cards for each hero. It's a shame, because they have plenty of other avenues for monetization. They have skins for the captains which I'd happily purchase if I wasn't pissed by the rest of the business model and they could probably do some other things like maybe skins for cards or... idk... maybe a board background? I really hope they will fix these issues. I think there is a good core game here and I really don't want to see it dragged down by a few poor decisions. There have definitely been other autobattlers and CCGs which I have put a lot of time into which I eventually rage quit over unaddressed issues like these. I will certainly come back and change my review if these get fixed.

Obviously I've played this a few hours. It's a decent mindless time-waster and the card art is very appealing. I'm giving it a Not Recommended for two reasons: 1. At higher levels (easily reached), most opponents have outrageously lucky boards, such that there is often no way to get above 4th place unless you get an outrageously lucky board yourself. 2. The developers' petty grandstanding about AI. It's a very bad precedent to use news boxes for this purpose.
It's an interpretation of a wonderful style of autobattler, and interesting, but very poorly balanced.

More rerolls could help, plenty of options.

I enjoyed this game for the first 15 hours I played this, but I reached a point where I'm just done with the game. Here's my journey through playing this game. First time you play this game it's clearly a mobile game interface but it plays similarly to other card based autobattlers. It's very easy to miss tutorial popups playing on PC and there is no way to ever see them again if you miss it, you just have to learn by trial and error if you miss the popup. Matches are quick in this game and it's very quick to start a new match, which is very addictive and probably kept me playing 10 more hours than I should've played this. 10 hours in, I learn that you can drag your card to the top left to toss it. Massive failure of the interface for me to learn this so late, way after hitting legendary rank. 15 hours in, I learn Captains (the character you choose at the start of each match) for some reason have a customizable deck. Cool, except some of them I couldn't make a custom deck for, and also you have to play games on the captain to unlock cards for it, and cards you unlock on one captain are not unlocked for other captains. Very grindy and made me think that playing some captains is a noob trap because you need to unlock cards for it and grind losses otherwise. I realized very quickly that some captains are just straight up better than 90% of the other captains in the game (when your goal is to get 1st place). I found myself clicking the same few captains on repeat (the captains that either generate mass treasures, buff treasures or generate captains that then generate treasures) which eventally led to every game feeling very similar. You also generally see the same few captains in each game at legendary rank which also contributes to stagnant feeling games. The randomness in this game is so insane that you can go from dying (losing all 3 hearts) by turn 5 to bad hit rng (can cause you to lose a full heart in a turn), to winning by turn 20 (games typically end around turn 13) only because you found one random spell/treasure that allows you to high roll and significantly improve your board too late. Matches usually end up as you hitting 3rd place because the top 2 players high rolled with stats 3x as large as your board or you hitting 6th place because you low rolled, scaled up slightly too slowly, or got 2 turns where you were hit for a full heart (bad hit rng). The game eventually felt repetitive, frustrating, and it felt like I was just cranking a slot machine praying for good captain and hit rng so I stopped playing at 2973 mmr. I enjoyed my time with this game but probably ended up playing it too much to the point where I don't want to ever play it again. It's a good game but definitely something you have to pace yourself playing. Surprisingly it's difficult to not just click the play button after each game ends. Very addictive game.

At first I really liked this game. However, the more you play, the more you realize it's largely RNG. You face opponents from some random pool of previous players. Those players were almost always on insanely high roll runs. You will never face an opponent that's having a bad run (in my experience). From there it's a coin flip if you can even compete, let alone win. Now, I'm not saying "it's too hard", "it's not fair", or any other crybaby thing that people will want to put on me. There's just too many things that are completely up to RNG. 1. You get to pick from 2-3 random heroes (not always 3, if you haven't bought the third one). When you play a hero enough and win enough of their cards, you will get a silver portrait, instead of the bronze that you start with. I have never once seen a silver hero available to me during the monthly "tournament". 2. Opponents are picked through some sort of act of God. You just get what the code gives you, and that is never from someone that didn't have a great run. I understand that it sounds like whining about hard opponents, but it's not. It's become like The Bazaar, where the game never picks anyone other than the best. This means that if you start off slow, you're done. You have no chance to recover, because all your foes have high-rolled from turn one. 3. All too often you will have a hero with a card type specific skill. Be it character type, skill type, gold cards, or treasures (etc.), you will often times never see the cards you need. If your hero needs minions with "hunt", you may never see any, completely negating your hero. Again, if this was an uncommon occurrence, then bad luck could be the culprit. At the rate it happens though, it has to be more than that. Keep in mind, this will never happen to anyone you're facing. Unfortunately this game is all or nothing. If you aren't on par for a power build by turn two, you might as well start over. Just my $0.02 on it. I'm not trying to hate the game, but I also cannot recommend it. If you like RNG with choices, go for it.

Once Upon a Galaxy's a fun autobattler that comes from people with prior experience with them, and it looks pretty good! (and is morally good with the art credits and all; there's great art that doesn't look uncanny!) The balance right now is a little strange, but you can definitely just win with anybody; there's really strong moves you can do without a captain power, so thinking about how a new card can synergize with a captain is pretty fun as a thought exercise, and sometimes even more fun in practice. Also, Top 3 is where the rewards start, so that's pretty generous... There are unfortunately a few hitches at the moment. For one, card acquisition is a little strange, to the point where you sometimes get more after surrendering to a specific board lategame since the other person just didn't run any characters on boards that could be unlocks for any number of reasons! (Secret rares on opposing boards really should make another unlock happen; you're so incentivized to keep them!) Related to that, Boons have made games go up to a crazy fever pitch in record times; there's sometimes a Legendary on Turn 5 or so, and that sometimes *really* cramps you in particular up due to the nature of asynchronous lobbies. Despite all of that, there's a lot of fun just booting up to a Galaxy, playing into a specific style, and just jamming a few games out. It's great, you don't have to spend any money if you don't want to, but doing so does support the fine people that made the game. It sounds like a good enough deal, every once in a while! And balance patches happen at least on a bimonthly basis, so these balance issues will eventually just become less of a problem. Which is great.

The game is beautiful to look out, and card/hero themes are clever and add color to the game. However, sadly there are big problems that make it not live up the glory of it's predecessor (Storybook Brawl). Therefore, I cannot recommend it. And when I say sadly, I mean it. I loved SBB and really felt for the devs for what happened to that gem of a game. Maybe the problems in this game are due to that trauma, because SBB had none of these problems. [h1]Incongruent game design[/h1] Half of the design choices in this game are minimalist and the other half is complex/obscure. This is one of the best ways to create a game where only few players are fully happy about it. 1. The most major offender here is having deck building in an auto battler. This means you need to build a deck for each of the 85 heroes to play optimally. I find this extremely annoying. One of the selling points of auto battlers they skip the deck building hustle. But the combination is even worse! Because in a normal deck builder, after you invest time in building the deck, you can play with it a bunch of times or even tinker with it as you go along. This is impossible with a game where you can't choose your hero. So you end up editing the deck for 1 game! Really bad design choice. 2. Games are too short in the context of how the game is designed. This leads to a feeling the games end "mid build" before you reach the payoffs you were aiming for. 3. You don't have a stash for cards to keep for later. Given how short the game is, maybe this makes sense. But personally I am not a huge fan of this. It is minimalist while at the same time feeling more hard core, as there is less room for error in what you replace. In a way it's the embodiment of the incongruent design of this game - being minimalist and hard core at the same time in all the wrong ways. For me it's just isn't fun- You don't get the casual mindless fun of a casual design or the elaborate depth of a complex design. It just ends up being mildly annoying throughout the game. [h1]UI problems[/h1] 1. Spells have rarities but don't show a colored gem like all the other cards. Why?! A truly baffling choice. You have to click the card and then it shows the rarity in text with no gem either. Rarity gems make learning the game faster. Every time I look at a spell card I get annoyed at this. 2. The bank icon is almost completely invisible. I only discovered it by reading about it. Another extremely bizarre choice. 3. You can't see your enemies in the shop phase. Some rare cards give you a reward based on the enemy you will be facing. But you have no way of checking what enemies are still in the game. It is assumed you will remember that which 99& of players won't. 4. I run into a reward that says if I meet a certain condition I get 4 cards. But it isn't really clear what that means and because the game is so short I didn't get to fins out. Not fun. 5. Some cards with key words have the keywords spelled out on the card negating the whole idea of having keywords in the first place and makes these cards busy for no reason. 6. There are certain words in the text with emphasis, but it is so subtle it hard to see it at all making it useless. 7. Certain bonuses like +1 Fae bonuses are tracked invisibly. There is no place you can look to find where you stand with them. You can see the repeating pattern of having [b] complex design choices combined with a minimalist UI creating an obscure gameplay experience [/b]. 8. You cannot see the base stats of a characters after it has been buffed making it harder to learn the cards because as a noob you don't know if you are looking at a buffed version or not. Especially because shop characters can be buffed too. 9. Overall it looks like this was mostly aimed at mobile leading to the layout not feeling/looking so great on a PC. 10. Even though the game is async you can't stop a run and continue it later like in other async games. WHY?! Did I say baffling already? There are other things that are just not clear enough AND/OR don't feel right. [h1]Game does a bad job of explaining itself[/h1] You basically have to go read the rules to figure it out, and even then some interactions are still unclear. For example buffs are permanent everywhere. Even if you sell a character and get it back later. But it doesn't say so anywhere in game. There were other occasions where things hapend that I just could not explain. I do not know if this is because of interactions I wasn't aware of or due to bugs. At least some case are suspect as bugs, as the behavior made no sense (for example: quest card giving treasure but still have counter on it. Then when counter ended nothing happened) TLDR This game failed to choose if it's a casual low investment game or a hard core "google the best deck" kind of game. For me it ended up failing on both the casual and hard core experience. In addition the UI has many clarity issues that detract from the experience.

the most astonishingly free to play friendly game of all time. the amount of characters and content you get from jump is more than enough to keep you entertained for hours. it hits that perfect balance in an auto battler where you have to be intentional and work for your synergies, but once your build gets online it can get uber powerful. of course you'll encounter a lot of other strong builds, but there's a lower rate of just impossible to beat builds compared to similar games like the bazaar or battlegrounds. quick to learn, respects your time, with a pleasing theme and art. definitely worth a download

180 hours of trying to convince myself things will get better. The system is currently set up to tie your hands and rely on pure luck in order to win. Your deck consist of 12 cards and they force you to fish for those 12 cards amongst 126 community cards. If you get what you need you can have a good game. if you get part of what you need you will probably get a top 3. The issue is that you only get what you need maybe 10% of the time. This might not sound THAT bad until you realize their system for your opponents. snapshots of other people who had good games. occasionally you might get an early win here and there, but if you don't, you can bet your sweet tooshy that your opponent after turn 12 will most likely have their perfect hand with all the cards and treasures they could ever want. Then there's the MMR system. Anyone can climb it slowly but surely. in my 2 months i climbed to 2300, but i also played a LOT. the issue is, you get fewer points for a win than you lose for finishing 5th or 6th. " so just don't be bad" right? Well remember the whole needing at least some of your cards to get that top 3? a lot of the times not only do you get nothing you need, your opponents still do get everything they need. it will give you nothing but 1/1-1/3 cards for 5 shops in a row and you are helpless and get forced out on turn 4 or 5 with absolutely nothing you could have done differently to change the outcome. I record everything with medal. i have spent an unhealthy amount of time watching the games thinking it was me messing up. Once you get past the learning curve of knowing situational things to do, the metas everyone plays, and reading enough tips from others, you are just stuck in a loop of winning 30%, getting top 3 30% and getting force lossed 30%, so your MMR creeps up slowly. an illusion to think you are getting better, but at the end of the day you are just helpless to the system. even if you get the perfect draws and make the right plays. you will still lose to some gimmick that only works with tiny chance combination of treasures and abilities. all the treasures are RNG, you can do 3 quests and get nothing but lucky chests, skeleton keys, and villain/hero specific treasures you cant even use. all the spells are RNG. you can go multiple games without ever seeing a shrink tea, midnight, or even a true loves kiss. you can play a villain captain and get nothing but fae. you can play a candy captain and go 20 shops without seeing a candy spell. the whole thing is a giant bundle of chaos, and until there is more consistency and ability to actually play the game mechanically instead of relying on chance, I can't recommend it.

I want to preface this by saying that the game is genuinely fun, and I do actually enjoy quite a bit. There is just one major problem that stops me from recommending this game: there are too many captains and too many of them are either mediocre or downright bad. The game desperately needs a favored captain selection or something to let the player choose from a pool of captains they actually want to play rather than strictly relying on RNG to hand them a good option every game. It feels really bad to be handed a string of captains you don't like playing multiple games in a row, and it feels even worse during tournaments where your chance of winning is entirely dependent on captain RNG not being dogwater. In a lot of instances it feels like the game is deciding whether or not you're allowed to win. This isn't strictly an issue of "all of the captains I was handed are bad" either. Since building a deck is part of the game, you have to deck build for *every single captain* if you want to be able to play them at all competently. And you have to unlock cards for *every single captain*. Captains don't share card pools, so even if you have a generically good decklist that should work with any captain, you can't use it on every captain unless they have all the cards. It's a frustrating aspect of an otherwise good game.

Developed and published by Million Dreams Games, Once Upon a Galaxy presents a creative spin on the auto battler genre by merging fairy tale inspirations with a sprawling science-fiction backdrop. Rather than relying on traditional fantasy kingdoms or gritty futuristic settings, the game imagines a universe where legendary figures and storybook personalities travel through space in search of victory. This unusual combination gives the title a memorable identity from the very beginning, helping it distinguish itself from the crowded landscape of multiplayer strategy games available on Steam. At its core, the game revolves around assembling a team of heroes under the command of a Captain, whose unique abilities influence every decision throughout a match. Players recruit companions, discover magical artifacts, and cast spells while adapting to constantly changing circumstances. The gameplay is intentionally easy to understand, making it approachable for newcomers, but beneath its accessible surface lies a respectable amount of strategic depth. Building effective combinations, managing resources, and responding to opponents' tactics become increasingly important as players gain experience. The six-player competitive structure keeps matches dynamic, ensuring that no session unfolds exactly the same way twice. The game's greatest strength is its commitment to variety. Each Captain encourages different playstyles, while the extensive roster of units and items opens the door to countless combinations. Whether players prefer aggressive strategies, defensive setups, or carefully engineered synergies, Once Upon a Galaxy provides the tools to experiment. This replayability is further enhanced by the unpredictability of each run, as available recruits and treasures can dramatically shift the direction of a match. While chance plays a role, skilled players who understand the game's systems will consistently find opportunities to improve their odds and outmaneuver competitors. Visually, Once Upon a Galaxy embraces a colorful and inviting presentation that complements its whimsical premise. Character designs are expressive and distinctive, making it easy to identify favorite units while appreciating the game's playful interpretation of folklore in a cosmic setting. The interface is clean and functional, allowing players to focus on strategic decisions without unnecessary distractions. Combined with energetic animations and a lighthearted atmosphere, the game succeeds in creating an experience that feels welcoming without sacrificing its competitive edge. As a free-to-play title, the game benefits from a model that encourages players to jump in with minimal commitment. Million Dreams Games appears committed to supporting the experience through updates and seasonal content, which is particularly important for maintaining a healthy multiplayer community. Ongoing additions and balance adjustments have the potential to keep the metagame evolving over time, giving long-term players fresh reasons to return. However, those seeking a heavily narrative adventure may find the game's emphasis on multiplayer progression and replayability somewhat limiting. Similarly, newer players may initially struggle against veterans who have mastered optimal strategies and unit synergies. Once Upon a Galaxy ultimately succeeds by delivering an imaginative and polished take on familiar mechanics. Its combination of auto battler gameplay, collectible card elements, and fairy tale-inspired worldbuilding results in a package that feels both accessible and rewarding. While it occasionally leans on genre conventions and carries the expected learning curve of competitive strategy games, its charm, replay value, and strategic possibilities make it an enjoyable experience for fans of multiplayer titles. For players interested in discovering a distinctive blend of fantasy and science fiction wrapped in a fast-paced competitive format, Once Upon a Galaxy proves to be a worthwhile journey among the stars. Rating: 7/10

I used to love this game. The whimsical card design and the asynchronous battles have been a major selling point for me. It felt fun and refreshing and you certainly did not need to spend any money to be competitive. This made any pass purchase feel like you were supporting the dev team for a job well done. Unfortunately, the game is now at a state where multiple captains are dumped in the game every month, making this increasingly daunting for new players. As the, inevitably, imbalanced captain pool grows, f2p players will be stuck with considerably worse captains or a vastly diluted card pool, meaning their chances of winning diminish with every passing month. Worst of all though, and the reason why I am uninstalling, is because the dev team has introduced P2W elements in the shop in the form of reroll. This is an incremental benefit, as the captain pool is ever-expanding, but those who do not purchase the reroll system (which is per card set) are immediately worse off. I wish the game stayed more f2p friendly and less predatory, but unfortunately the trajectory the game has taken means this will only cater to whales. And there are more established card games for whales out there.
